analogy.p: Think of the soil as a loose tablecloth on a windy table, and plants as the plates and cutlery holding it down. If you start removing plates (cutting trees, grazing grass) the cloth lifts at the corners and is blown off, and once it has gone you cannot simply lay it back. The analogy shows how plants anchor the soil and how loss accelerates once protection is removed. It breaks down because a tablecloth is just blown away once, whereas desertification is a feedback loop in which a bare soil also makes it harder for new plants to grow.
analogy.t: A tablecloth held down by the plants

bullets: **Desertification** = the degradation of land in dry areas so that it becomes more like a desert (less vegetation, poorer soil, less water).
Areas at risk are the **semi-arid margins of hot deserts**, where there is just enough rain for grass and scrub but little margin for error.

The best-known example is the **Sahel** in Africa, the broad belt of semi-arid land along the southern edge of the Sahara desert, running across countries such as Mauritania, Mali, Niger, Chad and Sudan.
Other areas at risk include the margins of the Thar Desert in India, parts of Central Asia, Australia and the south-western USA.
Rainfall in these areas is low and **unreliable** (it varies a lot from year to year), so a run of dry years can tip the land into degradation.
Roughly one in six people in the world is affected by land degradation in dry areas, and the people most at risk are often poor farmers who depend directly on the land.
It links to Topic 1.4 (hot desert characteristics): the thin soils, sparse plants and low rainfall of hot deserts are exactly why the margins are so fragile.
core.h: What desertification is and where it happens
core.p: **Desertification** is the process by which fertile land becomes desert-like and unable to support plants, animals or people. It is a form of **land degradation** that happens in **arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas**, mostly on the edges of existing hot deserts, where rainfall is low and unreliable and the vegetation is already sparse. It is not simply the desert 'marching' forward like a wave of sand; instead the land loses its plant cover and its soil, so it begins to behave like a desert. Because the loss of plants and soil is very hard to reverse, desertification is a serious threat to food supply and livelihoods.

bullets: Step 1: **vegetation is removed or reduced** (grazing, wood cutting, ploughing, drought).
Step 2: the soil is left **bare and exposed**; plant roots no longer bind the soil particles together.
Step 3: without leaf cover, heavy rain hits the soil directly, and the dry loose soil is blown away by wind: **soil erosion**.
Step 4: the nutrient-rich **topsoil is lost**, so the soil is thinner, less fertile and holds less water (infiltration is poor and run-off is high).
Step 5: **fewer plants can grow**, and crop yields and grazing fall, so people and animals stress the remaining land even more.
This is a **positive feedback** loop, because the output of the process (less vegetation) feeds back to make the original problem (soil loss) worse.
Dry soil that is baked hard in the sun also repels water, so more rain runs off rather than soaking in, which starves plants even further.
core.h: The vicious cycle: how land turns to desert
core.p: Desertification works as a **positive feedback loop** (a vicious cycle) in which each step makes the next one worse. Plants are removed or die, which leaves the soil bare. Without roots to bind it and leaves to shelter it, the soil is easily eroded by wind and by the rare heavy rainstorms. The topsoil, which holds most of the nutrients and humus, is lost, so fewer plants can grow back, and the cycle repeats with ever poorer land. Understanding this chain is the key to explaining any cause of desertification in an exam.

bullets: Rising temperatures increase **evaporation**, drying the soil and reducing the water available to plants.
Reduced and **less reliable rainfall** means crops fail and natural vegetation dies back.
**Droughts** (long periods with little or no rain) kill plants and leave soil bare and loose.
Heavy rain on dry hard soil causes **flash floods and run-off**, which wash away topsoil rather than recharging soil moisture.
Climate change shifts rainfall belts, so some semi-arid areas that used to receive enough rain now receive too little.
Climate change acts as a **trigger or multiplier**: it makes land more vulnerable, but human activities (below) usually decide how severe the damage is.
Exam tip: link the cause to the effect, for example 'less rainfall so vegetation dies, so soil is exposed to erosion'.
core.p: Climate change is a **natural and human-influenced** cause of desertification. In many dry regions the climate has become warmer and rainfall has become lower or more variable. Higher temperatures increase **evaporation** and **transpiration**, so soils dry out faster, while longer and more frequent **droughts** kill off plants that cannot survive without water. When rain does come it can fall in short, intense storms that cause run-off and erosion rather than soaking in. In the Sahel the severe droughts of the 1970s and 1980s were a major trigger of land degradation, made worse by human pressure on the land.

bullets: More people means greater **demand for food, water, and fuel** from a fragile environment.
Pressure leads to **more livestock, more fields, and more trees cut**: population growth is the root of the other human causes.
Land is farmed continuously, so **fallow periods are shortened** and soils cannot recover.
Settlements and wells attract people and animals, so land around water points can be heavily degraded.
Many people in these regions are **poor and have few alternatives**, so they cannot afford fertiliser or to stop using damaged land.
Population growth plus a less reliable climate is a particularly dangerous combination.
Link: more people leads to more fuelwood use, more grazing, and more cultivation, all of which remove vegetation.
core.p: A rising population in dry areas means more people need food, water, fuel and shelter from the same limited land. As population grows, each family tries to grow more crops and keep more animals, and the land is used more intensively and for longer without a rest. Population growth does not cause desertification directly; it works by increasing the pressure that causes **overgrazing, over-cultivation and fuelwood removal**, which is why it is an underlying cause. Sahel countries have some of the highest population growth rates in the world, so the pressure on fragile land is increasing.

bullets: Many families use **wood as the main fuel** for cooking, so large numbers of trees and shrubs are cut.
Trees are cut faster than they can **regenerate** in a dry climate with slow growth.
Roots that once **bound the soil** are lost, so the soil is loosened and blown or washed away.
Loss of shade means **more evaporation** from the soil surface and a hotter ground temperature.
Loss of leaf litter reduces **organic matter (humus)** so the soil becomes less fertile and less able to hold water.
Villages must travel **further each year** to find wood, spreading the damaged area outwards in rings around settlements.
Solutions include solar cookers and fuel-efficient stoves, covered later in appropriate technology.
core.p: In many hot desert margins people rely on **wood and charcoal for cooking and heating** because they cannot afford gas or electricity and there is no alternative. Trees and shrubs are cut faster than they can regrow, so the land is stripped of its plant cover. Trees are especially valuable because their deep roots bind the soil, their leaves shade the ground and reduce evaporation, and their leaf litter adds nutrients (humus). When they are removed all of these protections are lost, and the ground is open to wind erosion.

bullets: **Overgrazing** = too many animals for the amount of vegetation, so plants cannot recover.
Livestock **eat the grass and shrubs** that protect the soil, leaving bare patches.
Hooves **trample and compact the soil**, making it harder for water to soak in (more run-off) and harder for seeds to germinate.
Grazing around wells and water points is most intense, producing **sacrifice zones** of bare ground.
Herds are a measure of wealth and security, so families are reluctant to reduce their size even when pasture is poor.
Bare, trampled soil is easily blown away, and gullies can form where run-off concentrates.
Goats and camels can strip shrubs and tree leaves, removing even the deep-rooted vegetation that survives in droughts.
core.p: **Overgrazing** happens when too many animals such as cattle, goats, sheep and camels feed on an area, so plants are eaten faster than they can regrow. The animals also **trample and compact** the soil, which reduces infiltration and increases run-off. Goats are especially damaging because they eat shrubs down to the roots and even climb trees. Once the plant cover is gone the soil is bare, and wind and water can erode it, starting the vicious cycle. Nomadic herders who once moved often now settle for longer because of boundaries or wells, which concentrates grazing.

bullets: **Over-cultivation** = growing too many crops on the land without allowing it to recover.
Crops remove nutrients faster than they are replaced, so the soil becomes **infertile and exhausted**.
Ploughing leaves the soil **loose and bare** between crops, ready to be blown away by wind.
Cultivating land too close to the edge of the desert (marginal land) means crops fail in dry years and leave the soil bare.
**Soil erosion** by wind (deflation) removes fine particles; erosion by water (rills and gullies) carries soil away during storms.
Eroded soil is **very slow to form** (centuries per centimetre), so the loss is effectively permanent on human timescales.
Poor irrigation can cause **salinisation**: water evaporates and leaves salts in the topsoil, making it too salty for crops.
core.p: **Over-cultivation** means growing crops too intensively on the same land, without enough rest or nutrients being returned. Crops take nutrients out of the soil, and in dry areas the natural supply of nutrients is already very low. If farmers do not leave land fallow, rotate crops or add manure and fertiliser, the soil becomes exhausted, crop yields fall, and the land is abandoned as bare ground. Ploughing also breaks up the soil surface and removes the natural plant cover, making it easier to be eroded. The end result of all the causes is **soil erosion**, which is the removal of the topsoil by wind and water, and it is the process that actually turns degraded land into desert.

bullets: **Terracing**: building steps on slopes slows run-off so water soaks in and soil is not washed downhill.
**Contour ploughing and stone lines**: rows of stones or bunds built along the contour trap water and soil, increasing infiltration and crop yields.
**Zai pits / planting pits**: small holes filled with manure collect rainwater and nutrients for each plant, used in Burkina Faso and Niger.
**Mulching and crop rotation** protect the soil surface, add organic matter and keep nutrients balanced.
**Rainwater harvesting** (small dams, tanks, and underground storage) stores water in the wet season for use in the dry season.
**Drip irrigation** delivers small amounts of water directly to roots, reducing evaporation and salinisation.
These methods are **low cost, sustainable and use local labour**, so they suit poor communities and can be maintained without outside help.
core.h: Reducing the risk 1: water and soil management
core.p: The aim of water and soil management is to **catch and keep water** in the soil, and to **hold the soil in place**, so that plants can grow and the land can recover. Many of these methods are cheap, use local materials and can be done by farmers themselves. They work by slowing run-off, increasing infiltration, and protecting the soil surface from wind and rain. Examples are used widely in the Sahel and in dry regions of India.

bullets: **Tree roots bind the soil**, reducing both wind and water erosion.
**Shelter belts** (lines of trees along field edges) slow the wind, protecting crops and topsoil.
Leaves and branches **shade the soil**, reducing evaporation, and leaf litter returns nutrients, so soil structure improves.
**Agroforestry** mixes trees and crops on the same land, giving shade, fuel, fruit, animal fodder and soil protection together.
The **Great Green Wall** is a project to plant a belt of trees and restore land across the Sahel, from Senegal to Djibouti.
Trees need protection from grazing animals and watering at first; community involvement is vital for success.
Limitations: trees take years to grow, young plants may die in drought, and the large-scale schemes can be expensive.
core.p: Planting trees and shrubs restores the natural protection that vegetation gives the soil. Roots bind the soil, leaves reduce the impact of rain and shade the ground, and fallen leaves add nutrients. Trees also act as **windbreaks or shelter belts**, which slow the wind and cut wind erosion across fields. In some places farmers are supported to protect and regrow trees that already exist in their fields, which is cheaper than planting new ones. Species chosen must be **drought-resistant and suited to local conditions**, otherwise the seedlings die.

bullets: **Solar cookers and fuel-efficient stoves** cut the amount of wood needed, which reduces tree cutting.
**Hand-dug wells and small-scale pumps (including solar pumps)** provide water without large costly projects.
**Low-cost drip irrigation kits** and simple rainwater tanks use water efficiently.
Local materials such as stones, clay and manure keep costs low and mean repairs are possible locally.
The community is involved in planning, building and running the project, so it is **sustainable** and fits local culture.
Because it is small scale it has **less environmental impact** than large dams or machines and can be spread to many villages.
Evaluate: small projects may only help a few families, and without training or spare parts equipment can fail.
core.p: **Appropriate technology** (also called intermediate technology) means technology that is simple, cheap, easy to maintain and suited to the skills, resources and needs of local people. It does not rely on expensive imported machinery or outside experts, so communities can run it themselves and keep it going. In desertification areas, appropriate technology reduces the pressure that causes the problem, for example by cutting the need for fuelwood or making better use of scarce water.

bullets: **Opportunity: farming**. The **Indira Gandhi Canal** carries water from Punjab's rivers into the north-west Thar, so irrigation allows crops such as wheat, cotton and mustard to be grown where it was once impossible.
**Opportunity: mineral extraction**. Rajasthan has deposits of **gypsum, limestone and sandstone**, and oil is produced in the Barmer area, providing jobs and income.
**Opportunity: energy**. Hot sunny, clear days and strong winds make the Thar ideal for **solar power and wind farms**, such as the huge Bhadla Solar Park and wind farms near Jaisalmer.
**Opportunity: tourism**. Jaisalmer's fort, camel safaris, desert festivals, and traditional culture attract visitors and bring money to local people.
**Challenge: extreme temperatures**. Heat stress and dehydration affect health, outdoor work is difficult, and building and machinery need to cope with the heat.
**Challenge: water supply**. Rainfall is low, groundwater is being used faster than it is replaced, and the canal supply is costly; poor irrigation can cause waterlogging and salinisation.
**Challenge: inaccessibility**. Settlements are far apart, shifting sand covers roads, and building roads, pipelines and power lines is difficult and expensive.
Population pressure and heavy grazing in the Thar also mean the area is **at risk of desertification** itself, linking the case study to the rest of this topic.
core.h: Case study: a hot desert environment (the Thar Desert, India)
core.p: The **Thar Desert** (the Great Indian Desert) lies mainly in the Indian state of **Rajasthan**, extending into Pakistan. It is a hot desert with extreme summer temperatures that often exceed 45 degrees Celsius, very low and unreliable rainfall (under about 250 mm a year in the driest west) and sandy, thin soils. Unlike many deserts it is **densely populated**, so there is intense pressure on land and water. The case study you need is about how people use the hot desert environment (**opportunities**) and the problems they face (**challenges**). Your school may have taught the Sahara instead, in which case use the same structure with that place's facts.

bullets: **Economic benefits**: jobs, income, improved infrastructure (roads, electricity) and the chance for people to move out of subsistence farming.
**Social benefits**: better access to water, health and education when new settlements and canals are built.
**Environmental costs**: waterlogging and **salinisation** from poor irrigation, lowering of the water table, and habitat loss from mines and solar farms.
**Water is the limiting factor**: any development must plan for how much water is really available over the long term.
**Sustainable development** in the desert means using water carefully (e.g. drip irrigation), protecting soil and vegetation, and involving local communities.
Different groups gain and lose differently: companies and tourists may benefit more than traditional herders.
In an evaluation use words such as 'however', 'on the other hand' and 'overall, the most significant is...' to show judgement.
core.h: Evaluating development and sustainability in hot deserts
core.p: Higher-mark questions ask you to weigh up benefits against problems and to judge whether development is **sustainable**, meaning it meets present needs without damaging the ability of future generations to meet theirs. Irrigation can transform farming and income, but if water is taken faster than it is replaced, groundwater will run out and soils may be ruined by salt. Energy and mineral projects bring jobs and money but can scar the landscape and may not employ many local people. A good answer weighs both sides, uses case-study detail, and reaches a supported judgement.

bullets: Link back to **hot desert characteristics** (climate, soil, vegetation, adaptations) to explain why margins are fragile.
Link to **climate change** (Paper 1 section on the changing climate): more drought is likely in some regions.
Link to **sustainability and management**: each solution should be assessed for cost, effectiveness and long-term effect.
Link to **development and poverty**: poor communities have the least capacity to manage land well.
In questions on causes, always give the **mechanism** (what happens and why that causes degradation).
In questions on solutions, state the method, **how it works**, and a **limitation** for the highest marks.
Use specific place names and figures from your case study; unspecific answers cap at the lower mark band.
core.h: Linking to the wider topic and exam use
core.p: This spec point sits within The living world and connects ecosystems, climate and human activity. Desertification links physical geography (climate, soils, vegetation) to human geography (population, farming, poverty, development). Examiners like answers that show these links, such as how drought and overgrazing interact, or how a solution deals with a specific cause. The case-study content is also used in 6-mark questions on the opportunities and challenges for development in a hot desert.

exam: 'Describe' questions (usually 2 marks): state features, do not explain. For example, 'Desertification is the process of land turning into desert; vegetation and soil quality decline'.
'Explain' questions (3-4 marks): use the pattern point + reason + consequence. For example, 'Overgrazing removes plants (1), so soil is bare (1), and is eroded by wind and rain (1)'.
For 'Explain one cause of desertification' (usually 3 marks), pick one cause and develop it over three linked steps rather than listing several causes.
The six AQA causes are climate change, population growth, removal of fuel wood, overgrazing, over-cultivation and soil erosion; learn all six with their mechanisms.
The three solutions are water and soil management, tree planting and appropriate technology; for each give a method, how it works, and (for top marks) a limitation.

For 6-mark case-study questions (opportunities and challenges), use at least three opportunities and challenges with named place details (canal, solar park, temperatures), and finish with a conclusion.
Use command word cues: 'assess' and 'evaluate' need both sides and a judgement; 'suggest' means apply knowledge to a new situation or resource.
For figure or data questions quote values with units (e.g. 'rainfall fell from 250 mm to 200 mm'), and calculate percentage change if asked: change divided by original times 100.
Always link the cause to the effect on the land: 'less vegetation, so more erosion' is the key chain that earns marks.
Check you answer the actual question: 'reduce the risk' needs solutions, 'causes' needs reasons, 'case study' needs named facts.

mistakes.r: It is land degradation in dry areas where vegetation and soil are lost, so the land becomes like desert; the cause is the loss of plant cover and soil, not just sand moving.
mistakes.w: Desertification is when the desert spreads because of sand blowing over fields.

mistakes.r: Needs the chain: too many animals remove vegetation and trample soil, so soil is exposed and eroded by wind and water, and fewer plants regrow.
Say how: more people need more food and fuel, leading to more grazing, cultivation and wood cutting, which remove vegetation.
Cutting trees removes roots that bind the soil, shade and leaf litter, so the soil is exposed and eroded, and fuelwood is removed faster than regrowth.
mistakes.w: Cutting down trees means there is less oxygen.

mistakes.r: Terracing slows run-off on slopes, trapping water and soil; shelter belts (trees) reduce wind.
mistakes.w: Terracing is used to stop the wind.

mistakes.r: It means simple, cheap technology that suits local people's skills and can be maintained locally.
Name the desert, and give specific details such as the Indira Gandhi Canal, Bhadla Solar Park, temperatures over 45 degrees Celsius, and Jaisalmer tourism.
mistakes.w: Case study: 'the desert is hot and has no water' with no place facts.

mistakes.r: Evaluate: it increases yields but can cause salinisation, waterlogging and falling groundwater if the water is used unsustainably.
mistakes.w: Irrigation is only good for farmers.

summary: The spec asks you to explain what desertification is, its causes (climate change, population growth, removal of fuel wood, overgrazing, over-cultivation and soil erosion), how the risk can be reduced (water and soil management, tree planting, appropriate technology), and to know a hot desert case study with its opportunities and challenges. It matters because it shows how people and the environment interact in fragile dry lands and it is regularly tested with 4 and 6 mark questions.

terms.d: The process by which land in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas becomes degraded and turns into desert.
A decline in the quality of land, including loss of soil, vegetation and fertility, so it can no longer support the same use.
The semi-arid belt of Africa on the southern edge of the Sahara desert, which is at high risk of desertification.
Too many animals grazing on an area so that vegetation is eaten faster than it can regrow.
Growing crops too intensively so that soil nutrients are used up and the soil becomes infertile.
The removal of topsoil by wind and water.
Wood (and charcoal) collected from trees and shrubs to be used for cooking and heating.
A process in which a change causes further change in the same direction, so a problem speeds up.
Building steps into a slope to slow run-off, trap water and reduce soil erosion.
A line of trees planted to reduce wind speed and protect soil and crops.
Simple, low-cost technology that suits local skills, resources and needs and can be maintained by local people.
The build-up of salts in the soil, often caused by irrigation and evaporation, which reduces crop growth.
Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
Supplying water to land artificially so crops can grow where rainfall is not enough.
Land at the edge of what can be farmed, where small changes in rainfall cause crops to fail.

worked.ans: Overgrazing is when too many animals feed on the land, so vegetation is eaten faster than it regrows (1). This leaves the soil bare and trampled, so it is easily eroded by wind and rain and the land becomes infertile (1). Removal of fuel wood happens when people cut trees and shrubs for cooking (1). The roots no longer bind the soil, so it is blown or washed away, which leaves land that cannot support plants (1). (4 marks)
worked.q: Explain two causes of desertification. (4 marks)
steps: Choose two causes from the six in the spec, such as overgrazing and removal of fuel wood.
For each, give the cause (1 mark) and develop it with a reason or consequence (1 mark).
Make the link to soil exposure and erosion explicit.

worked.ans: Percentage decrease = (50 / 250) x 100 = 20 percent (2 marks). Less rainfall means less water for plants so vegetation dies, leaving bare soil that is easily eroded (1). (3 marks)
worked.q: Annual rainfall in a semi-arid area fell from 250 mm to 200 mm. Calculate the percentage decrease and suggest how this could increase the risk of desertification. (3 marks)
steps: Link lower rainfall to fewer plants, bare soil and erosion.

worked.ans: In the Thar Desert there are opportunities in farming, energy and tourism. The Indira Gandhi Canal brings water from Punjab so crops such as wheat and cotton can be grown, raising incomes. The sunny, windy climate suits solar power, for example Bhadla Solar Park, creating jobs and electricity. Tourism in Jaisalmer, with its fort and camel safaris, also brings money. However there are challenges. Summer temperatures above 45 degrees Celsius cause heat stress and make construction and outdoor work difficult. Water is scarce, groundwater is falling, and irrigation can cause salinisation. The area is remote, with shifting sand, so building roads and power lines is costly. Overall the opportunities are significant, but water supply is the main limit, so development will only be sustainable if water is managed carefully (6 marks).
worked.q: Using a case study of a hot desert environment, assess the opportunities and challenges for development. (6 marks)
steps: Name the desert (Thar, Rajasthan, India) and give two or three opportunities with detail.
Give two or three challenges with detail.
Add a judgement about which outweighs the other and why.
